definition: Values describing how one quantity varies with another, often a measurement over time. DSP commonly works on sequences of sampled values.
example: A temperature reading every second forms a time signal.

definition: Analysis or transformation of signals represented as numerical sequences. Tasks include measuring levels, finding patterns and filtering unwanted components.
One value of a signal at a specified position or time. The value alone does not specify its time spacing or physical units.
An integer identifying a sample’s position in a sequence. In these lessons the first sample has index zero; divide an index by the uniform sample rate to obtain time relative to the first sample.
Taking signal values at equally spaced times. A constant sample rate describes that spacing; irregular samples instead need their actual timestamps.
The number of equally spaced samples per second. It connects positions in a numerical sequence to physical time.
example: At 1000 samples per second, neighbouring samples are one millisecond apart.

definition: The time between neighbouring uniformly spaced samples, equal to the reciprocal of the sample rate.
In this course, the number of stored samples divided by their uniform sample rate: the duration of that many sample periods. It includes one period beyond the final sample’s timestamp.
The time from the first sample’s timestamp to the last sample’s timestamp. A non-empty record with five samples has four intervening gaps; an empty record has no such span.
The SI unit of time. Sample periods and record durations are expressed in seconds or fractions such as milliseconds.
One thousandth of a second. A sample rate of 1000 samples per second has a one-millisecond sample period.
The unit of frequency: one hertz means one cycle per second. One kilohertz is one thousand hertz; sample rates are also often written in hertz, with the meaning samples per second stated.
The volt is the unit of electrical potential difference, or voltage. A voltage signal’s mean, peak and RMS are all measured in volts.
A unit of power, the rate of energy transfer. A signal’s squared numerical values are not automatically watts; a physical relationship is needed.
A Python library for numerical arrays and operations on them. An arithmetic operation on a NumPy array commonly acts on all of its elements.
A Python library of scientific algorithms, including signal-processing operations. Its signal module provides filters, convolution and correlation routines with documented boundary conventions.
A smoothly repeating signal described by a sine or cosine function. Its amplitude, frequency and phase specify its height, repetition rate and position within a cycle.
Functions mapping an angle to perpendicular coordinates on the unit circle. Cosine gives the horizontal coordinate and sine the vertical coordinate; their values lie between −1 and +1.

The size of a signal or component, with the measurement convention stated. For an ideal sinusoid, amplitude usually means the maximum displacement from its centre; sampled peak or RMS are different measurements.
The repetition rate of a periodic signal, normally measured in cycles per second or hertz. Physical frequency depends on the time spacing of samples, not their values alone.

An angle identifying position within a signal cycle or the direction of a nonzero complex quantity. A phase shift is a difference between phase angles using the same convention. State degrees or radians and the chosen sine/cosine reference.
An angle unit equal to arc length divided by circle radius. A full circle is twice pi radians; Python’s sine and cosine functions take radians.
The constant ratio of a circle’s circumference to its diameter, approximately 3.14159. Twice pi radians is one full turn.

Frequency expressed relative to sampling rather than directly in hertz. This course distinguishes cycles per sample from radians per sample; other conventions may divide by the Nyquist frequency, so the convention must be stated.
Computer arithmetic representing numbers with finite precision and a variable scale. Rounded operations can leave tiny residual errors even when an exact mathematical result is zero.

Ambiguity caused when different original signal frequencies produce the same samples. Unwanted components can fold into a wanted frequency range, and a later filter cannot identify their original frequencies from those samples alone.

A frequency range beginning at zero, rather than a band centred around a higher carrier frequency. These lessons use the baseband sampling condition with all content strictly below half the sample rate.
An ideal signal having no frequency content outside a stated finite band. Real anti-alias filters approximate this restriction with finite attenuation and a transition region.
In this course, half the sample rate. Baseband signals must stay strictly below this frequency to preserve arbitrary sinusoidal phase at the edge under ideal sampling assumptions.

A filter applied before a sampling or sample-rate-reduction step to reduce frequencies that would otherwise alias into the retained band. Analogue acquisition needs this filtering before the relevant sampling step.
A device converting an analogue quantity into digital codes. Sampling restricts measurement times and quantisation restricts representable values; both choices affect the information retained.
A signal represented by a continuously variable physical quantity, such as voltage. An analogue signal must be appropriately filtered before sampling to control aliasing.
Mapping input values to a discrete set of representable levels. The resulting error depends on level spacing, rounding convention and whether an input exceeds the available range.
A binary digit with two possible states. Three bits can label eight codes, but code count alone does not specify the corresponding signal levels or rounding policy.
Restricting values beyond a permitted range to an endpoint. Different original values can then produce the same stored value, so lowering gain afterwards cannot recover their original heights.
The function returning the greatest integer no larger than its input. Unlike rounding towards zero, it maps −1.5 to −2.
A noise model with equal power per unit bandwidth over its stated frequency range. Quantisation error is not automatically white noise; its behaviour depends on the signal and quantiser.

The sum of a finite record’s sample values divided by its positive sample count. It retains the signal’s units and describes that record’s constant offset; it does not automatically reveal a permanent source bias.
The constant part of a signal, described for a finite record by its mean. DC originally means direct current, but the signal-processing idea also applies to other measured quantities.
The largest absolute sample value in a specified record. It measures an extreme rather than an average and can miss larger continuous-wave values between samples.
The non-negative square root of the average squared sample values. RMS includes any DC offset, avoids cancellation of opposite signs and retains the original signal’s units.
Addition of one term for each integer index in a stated finite range. Both the lower and upper limits are included; define the range before calculating the total.
The non-negative magnitude of a real number, ignoring its sign. The absolute values of −2 and +2 are both 2.

A logarithmic unit for a ratio: ten times the base-ten logarithm of a power ratio, or conventionally twenty times that of an amplitude ratio. The amplitude expression agrees with a physical power comparison when both powers use the same proportionality to amplitude squared.
A function asking which exponent of a chosen base produces a number. The base-ten logarithm of 100 is 2; real logarithms need a positive input.

The specified positive comparison value used when expressing a signal level as a ratio or in decibels. Amplitude references must state units and whether the measurement is peak, RMS or another quantity.

A digital signal level expressed relative to a stated full-scale reference. Peak and RMS metering conventions can differ, so a reproducible result names the reference rather than assuming a universal sine-RMS convention.
A multiplier applied to signal values. A gain magnitude above one increases amplitude; a negative real gain also reverses polarity.

In these lessons, sample-by-sample addition of time-aligned signals, possibly after applying individual gains. The inputs need compatible units, sample rates and timing; addition can exceed either input’s peak.
The sign orientation of a real signal. Multiplying by a negative gain reverses positive and negative values; it does not generally mean the same thing as an arbitrary time delay.
A margin between a signal’s peak and the largest permitted level. It gives reinforcing mixed peaks room before clipping.
A shift making a signal occur an integer number of samples later. Delay time is the sample count divided by the sample rate, and finite records need an explicit edge and output-length policy.
Treating a finite sequence as zero outside its stored index range. This boundary assumption differs from wrapping the end back to the start.
A shift that wraps values falling off one end of a finite record back to the other end. It differs from a physical delay with zero values outside the original record.
A number with real and imaginary components, representing two perpendicular coordinates. DSP uses complex numbers to retain amplitude and phase information together.
The horizontal component in a complex number’s coordinate representation. For the Python complex value 3+4j, the real part is 3.
The coefficient of the imaginary unit in a complex number, represented on the vertical axis. For 3+4j this coefficient is the real number 4.
The mathematical unit whose square is −1. These lessons write it as j; Python denotes imaginary literals with a trailing j, such as 4j.
The non-negative distance of a complex point from the origin, found by taking the square root of the sum of its squared real and imaginary components. Components 3 and 4 give magnitude 5.
The complex value obtained by keeping the real part and reversing the sign of the imaginary part. Conjugation preserves magnitude and reflects a complex point across the real axis.
A complex representation of magnitude and phase, visualised as an arrow from the origin. A rotating unit phasor has cosine and sine as its real and imaginary projections.

A sequence of scores obtained by shifting a template relative to data, multiplying aligned values and adding. With complex signals the template is conjugated; input order, lag sign and boundary policy must be specified.
A known sequence used as the pattern to search for in a longer signal. Correlation compares the template with data at different shifts.
The shift used to align a template with data. For SciPy correlate(data, template), positive lag places the template later in the data; an output array index is not automatically a lag.

Rescaling a measured signal or score using a stated comparison quantity. The divisor, boundary convention and behaviour for zero divisors must be given; normalised does not identify a unique algorithm.
The position where a collection has its largest value, rather than the largest value itself. NumPy argmax chooses the first such position when several values tie.
A range including one endpoint and excluding the other. These lessons include the record start and exclude the end one sample period after the final timestamp.
For a positive-frequency sinusoid, the sample rate divided by its frequency: the number of sampling intervals in one full cycle. The reciprocal is frequency in cycles per sample.
A deliberately chosen signal used to check an operation or measurement. A sinusoid with known amplitude and frequency can reveal a scaling or sample-rate error.
